claim: The Orco mutant line exhibited an 11-bp insertion and a 4-bp deletion in the second exon, resulting in a shifted reading frame.
source: This mutant line exhibited an 11-bp insertion and a 4-bp deletion in the second exon, resulting in a shifted reading frame (Figure 1A).
evidence: The claim is supported by sequencing data and visual representation in Figure 1A showing the genetic mutation.

claim: The Orco amino acid sequence showed a significant change mediated by an early stop codon.
source: The Orco amino acid sequence showed a significant change mediated by an early stop codon (Figure 1B).
evidence: The claim is supported by predicted protein structure analysis shown in Figure 1B.

claim: No off-target sites with a less-than-5-nt alignment mismatch were found from Exonerate searching results.
source: Neither did we find any off-target sites with a less-than-5-nt alignment mismatch from Exonerate searching results, nor did we find any off-target sites with a less-than-4-nt alignment mismatch from CHOPCHOP searching results.
evidence: The claim is supported by computational analysis using Exonerate and CHOPCHOP tools to search for off-target sites.

claim: No off-target sites with a less-than-4-nt alignment mismatch were found from CHOPCHOP searching results.
source: Neither did we find any off-target sites with a less-than-5-nt alignment mismatch from Exonerate searching results, nor did we find any off-target sites with a less-than-4-nt alignment mismatch from CHOPCHOP searching results.
evidence: The claim is supported by computational analysis using CHOPCHOP tool to search for off-target sites.

claim: No developmental differences were found between wildtype animals and KO when caterpillars were raised on leaf discs in Petri dishes.
source: Furthermore, we did not find any developmental differences between wildtype (WT) animals and KO when caterpillars were raised on leaf discs in Petri dishes (Figure 1—figure supplement 1)
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data comparing caterpillar development shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: No difference was found in the hatching rate of fertilized WT and KO eggs.
source: Furthermore, we did not find any developmental differences between wildtype (WT) animals and KO when caterpillars were raised on leaf discs in Petri dishes (Figure 1—figure supplement 1) or in the hatching rate of fertilized WT and KO eggs (Figure 1—figure supplement 2).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data comparing hatching rates shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2.

claim: A total of 34 ORNs were successfully identified in L3 WT caterpillar antennae.
source: In L3 WT caterpillar antennae, a total of 34 ORNs were successfully identified (Wang et al., 2024; Figure 1C).
evidence: The claim is supported by immunostaining data shown in Figure 1C and cited previous work.

claim: No Orco-positive ORNs were found in the antennae of KO caterpillars.
source: However, no Orco-positive ORNs were found in the antennae of KO caterpillars (Figure 1D).
evidence: The claim is supported by immunostaining data shown in Figure 1D demonstrating absence of Orco-positive neurons.

claim: A low number of Orco-positive neurons were detected in the maxillary palps of L3 WT caterpillars.
source: Similarly, we detected a low number of Orco-positive neurons in the maxillary palps of L3 WT caterpillars (Figure 1E)
evidence: The claim is supported by immunostaining data shown in Figure 1E.

claim: No Orco-positive signal was detected in the maxillary palps of KO caterpillars.
source: Similarly, we detected a low number of Orco-positive neurons in the maxillary palps of L3 WT caterpillars (Figure 1E), but no Orco-positive signal was detected in the maxillary palps of KO caterpillars (Figure 1F).
evidence: The claim is supported by immunostaining data shown in Figure 1F demonstrating absence of Orco-positive signal.

claim: Glomeruli displayed well-defined shapes with clear boundaries in the WT LAC.
source: In the LAC, glomeruli displayed well-defined shapes with clear boundaries in the WT LAC (Figure 1G).
evidence: The claim is supported by confocal microscopy imaging shown in Figure 1G.

claim: In the KO LAC, the glomeruli were less clearly separated.
source: However, in the KO LAC, the glomeruli were less clearly separated (Figure 1H).
evidence: The claim is supported by confocal microscopy imaging shown in Figure 1H.

claim: Only 7–12 glomeruli were identified in KO LAC, which was a significant reduction compared to WT LAC.
source: Only 7–12 glomeruli were identified in KO LAC, which was a significant reduction (p = 0.0066, Wilcoxon rank-sum test) compared to WT LAC (Figure 1I).
evidence: The claim is supported by quantitative analysis of glomeruli counts with statistical testing shown in Figure 1I.

claim: Orco KO butterflies of both sexes displayed a complete loss of responses to most tested chemicals with the exception of isovaleric acid, n-caproic acid, hexanal, and 2,3-butanedione.
source: Orco KO butterflies of both sexes displayed a complete loss of responses to the tested chemicals with the exception of isovaleric acid, n-caproic acid, hexanal, and 2,3-butanedione, where no significant difference was detected between KO and WT butterflies.
evidence: The claim is supported by electroantennography (EAG) measurements comparing WT and KO butterflies.

claim: Reduced responses were recorded in KO butterflies to 1-nonanal, (Z)-2-pentenal, (E)-2-hexenal, and (Z)-3-hexenyl acetate.
source: Reduced responses were recorded in KO butterflies to 1-nonanal, (Z)-2-pentenal, (E)-2-hexenal, and (Z)-3-hexenyl acetate.
evidence: The claim is supported by electroantennography (EAG) measurements comparing WT and KO butterflies.

claim: WT male and female butterflies responded similarly to most of the volatile compounds with a few exceptions.
source: Besides, WT male (n = 18) and female (n = 15) butterflies responded similarly to most of the volatile compounds with a few exceptions where WT females showed significantly different responses to 2-methylbutanal (p = 0.0183, Kruskal–Wallis test), 3-methylbutanal (p = 0.0030, Kruskal–Wallis test), and 3-pentanone (p = 0.0263, Student's t-test) compared to KO females (n = 17), and WT males (n = 18) responded significantly stronger to acetic acid than KO males (p = 0.0217, Student's t-test).
evidence: The claim is supported by electroantennography (EAG) measurements with statistical comparisons.

claim: Both WT males and females showed no response to benzoic acid, methyl isothiocyanate (ITC), and 3-butenenitrile.
source: Moreover, both WT males and females showed no response to benzoic acid, methyl isothiocyanate (ITC), and 3-butenenitrile (p > 0.05, Student's t-test) (Figure 1J, K).
evidence: The claim is supported by electroantennography (EAG) measurements shown in Figure 1J and K.

claim: KO butterflies mated fewer times than WT butterflies.
source: Upon dissection, it was found that KO butterflies (n = 14) mated fewer times than WT butterflies (p = 0.0199, n = 11; Wilcoxon rank-sum test), since the majority of the KO butterflies (9 out of 14) did not mate during the experiment (Figure 1—figure supplement 3).
evidence: The claim is supported by dissection data and spermatophore counts with statistical testing shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 3.

claim: The majority of the KO butterflies (9 out of 14) did not mate during the experiment.
source: Upon dissection, it was found that KO butterflies (n = 14) mated fewer times than WT butterflies (p = 0.0199, n = 11; Wilcoxon rank-sum test), since the majority of the KO butterflies (9 out of 14) did not mate during the experiment (Figure 1—figure supplement 3).
evidence: The claim is supported by dissection data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 3.

claim: Out of the five KO butterflies that did mate, all but one mated singly.
source: Out of the five KO butterflies that did mate, all but one mated singly.
evidence: The claim is supported by dissection data counting spermatophores.

claim: Of the WT butterflies, 8 out of 11 mated, with most mating twice and one individual even thrice.
source: Of the WT butterflies, 8 out of 11 mated, with most mating twice and one individual even thrice.
evidence: The claim is supported by dissection data counting spermatophores.

claim: Female KO butterflies deposited fewer eggs than WT butterflies during the experiment.
source: Female KO butterflies also deposited fewer eggs than WT butterflies during the experiment (p < 0.0001, generalized linear model [GLM] negative binomial) (Figure 1—figure supplement 4).
evidence: The claim is supported by egg counting data with statistical testing shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 4.

claim: Virgin butterflies of both genotypes did not deposit any fertilized eggs.
source: It was found that virgin butterflies of both genotypes did not deposit any fertilized eggs, while mated butterflies exhibited similar fecundity with comparable hatching rates between the two genotypes without any significant difference (Figure 1—figure supplement 2).
evidence: The claim is supported by egg hatching data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2.

claim: Mated butterflies exhibited similar fecundity with comparable hatching rates between the two genotypes without any significant difference.
source: It was found that virgin butterflies of both genotypes did not deposit any fertilized eggs, while mated butterflies exhibited similar fecundity with comparable hatching rates between the two genotypes without any significant difference (Figure 1—figure supplement 2).
evidence: The claim is supported by egg hatching data with statistical testing shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2.

claim: In the absence of parasitoids, WT caterpillars exhibited better performance, gaining more weight compared to KO caterpillars.
source: The results show that in the absence of parasitoids, WT caterpillars exhibited better performance, gaining more weight compared to KO caterpillars (p = 0.0268, n = 17 for both genotypes; Student's t-test) (Figure 2A).
evidence: The claim is supported by caterpillar weight measurements with statistical testing shown in Figure 2A.

claim: No significant survival differences were found between the two genotypes while collecting caterpillars after the experiment.
source: However, we did not find significant survival differences between the two genotypes while collecting caterpillars after the experiment (WT mortality = 8.8 %, n = 17; KO mortality = 2. 9%; p = 0.0880, n = 17; Wilcoxon test).
evidence: The claim is supported by mortality data with statistical testing.

claim: There was no developmental difference when caterpillars were reared in a Petri dish supplied with leaf discs.
source: Nor was there a developmental difference when caterpillars were reared in a Petri dish supplied with leaf discs (p = 0.9698, n = 10 for both genotypes; Wilcoxon test) (Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by caterpillar weight measurements with statistical testing shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: Both genotypes of caterpillars chose the cabbage leaf disc significantly more often than the green paper discs.
source: Both genotypes of caterpillars chose the cabbage leaf disc significantly more often than the green paper discs (p = 0.0016 for KO, χ2 = 9.92; p < 0.0001 for WT, χ2 = 21.41; Chi-square test)
evidence: The claim is supported by behavioral choice data with statistical testing.

claim: No difference was detected between the two genotypes in choosing cabbage leaf disc over green paper disc.
source: Both genotypes of caterpillars chose the cabbage leaf disc significantly more often than the green paper discs (p = 0.0016 for KO, χ2 = 9.92; p < 0.0001 for WT, χ2 = 21.41; Chi-square test), and no difference was detected between the two genotypes (p = 0.1460, χ2 = 2.11; Chi-square test).
evidence: The claim is supported by behavioral choice data with statistical testing.

claim: When the cabbage leaf disc was replaced with a tomato leaf disc, both genotypes preferred the tomato leaf disc over the paper disc.
source: Similarly, when the cabbage leaf disc was replaced with a tomato leaf disc, both genotypes preferred the tomato leaf disc over the paper disc (p = 0.0143 for KO, χ2 = 6.00; p = 0.0009 for WT, χ2 = 10.97; Chi-square test)
evidence: The claim is supported by behavioral choice data with statistical testing.

claim: No difference was found between the two genotypes in choosing tomato leaf disc over paper disc.
source: Similarly, when the cabbage leaf disc was replaced with a tomato leaf disc, both genotypes preferred the tomato leaf disc over the paper disc (p = 0.0143 for KO, χ2 = 6.00; p = 0.0009 for WT, χ2 = 10.97; Chi-square test) and no difference was found between the two genotypes (p = 0.5477, χ2 = 0.36; Chi-square test).
evidence: The claim is supported by behavioral choice data with statistical testing.

claim: When caterpillars were provided with both a cabbage leaf disc and a tomato leaf disc, a contrasting preference was observed between the two genotypes.
source: However, when caterpillars were provided with both a cabbage leaf disc and a tomato leaf disc, a contrasting preference was observed between the two genotypes (p = 0.0004, χ2=12.68; Chi-square test).
evidence: The claim is supported by behavioral choice data with statistical testing.

claim: KO caterpillars significantly preferred the tomato leaf disc when provided with both cabbage and tomato leaf discs.
source: KO caterpillars significantly preferred the tomato leaf disc (p = 0.0466, χ2 = 3.96; Chi-square test)
evidence: The claim is supported by behavioral choice data with statistical testing.

claim: WT caterpillars preferred the cabbage leaf disc when provided with both cabbage and tomato leaf discs.
source: while WT caterpillars preferred the cabbage leaf disc (p = 0.0028, χ2=8.97; Chi-square test).
evidence: The claim is supported by behavioral choice data with statistical testing.

claim: WT caterpillars were significantly attracted by volatiles from a healthy plant.
source: Both WT and Orco KO caterpillars tended to prefer a healthy cabbage plant to a clean air control; however, WT caterpillars were significantly attracted by volatiles from a healthy plant (p = 0.0164, χ2 = 5.76; Chi-square test)
evidence: The claim is supported by Y-tube olfactometer behavioral data with statistical testing.

claim: The preference for Orco KO caterpillars toward healthy plant volatiles was not significant.
source: while the preference for Orco KO caterpillars was not significant (p = 0.2207, χ2 = 1.50; Chi-square test).
evidence: The claim is supported by Y-tube olfactometer behavioral data with statistical testing.

claim: WT caterpillars prefer volatiles from the infested plant to the control.
source: Subsequently, we challenged the caterpillars with volatiles from an infested plant and a clean air control and found that WT caterpillars prefer volatiles from the infested plant to the control (p = 0.0495, χ2 = 3.86; Chi-square test)
evidence: The claim is supported by Y-tube olfactometer behavioral data with statistical testing.

claim: Orco KO caterpillars did not show any preference between infested plant volatiles and clean air control.
source: while Orco KO caterpillars did not show any preference between the two provided options (p = 0.7055, χ2 = 0.14; Chi-square test).
evidence: The claim is supported by Y-tube olfactometer behavioral data with statistical testing.

claim: WT caterpillars showed a significant preference for infested plants without parasitoid wasps C. glomerata.
source: WT caterpillars showed a significant preference for infested plants without parasitoid wasps C. glomerata (p = 0.0067, χ2 = 7.35; Chi-square test)
evidence: The claim is supported by Y-tube olfactometer behavioral data with statistical testing.

claim: Orco KO caterpillars did not show any preference for either odor source when comparing infested plants with and without parasitoids.
source: while Orco KO caterpillars did not show any preference for either odor source (p = 0.7055, χ2 = 0.14; Chi-square test).
evidence: The claim is supported by Y-tube olfactometer behavioral data with statistical testing.

claim: WT caterpillars had significantly higher weight than KO caterpillars when exposed to parasitoids with removed ovipositors.
source: The results show a significantly higher weight in WT caterpillars than in KO caterpillars (p = 0.0088, n = 8 for both genotypes; Student's t-test).
evidence: The claim is supported by caterpillar weight measurements with statistical testing.

claim: KO caterpillars had significantly lower survival rates compared to WT caterpillars when exposed to unmanipulated parasitoids.
source: The findings show that KO caterpillars had significantly lower survival rates compared to WT caterpillars (p = 0.0120, n = 7 for both genotypes; GLM beta-binomial) (Figure 2F).
evidence: The claim is supported by survival rate data with statistical testing shown in Figure 2F.

claim: A total of 45 chemical compounds were identified among the five treatments belonging to seven classes.
source: We identified a total of 45 chemical compounds among the five treatments belonging to seven classes, including alcohols, aldehydes, aromatics, ketones, nitrogen and/or sulfur-containing chemicals, terpenoids, and others (Supplementary file 1A).
evidence: The claim is supported by volatile headspace analysis using GC-MS.

claim: Principal component analysis showed a significant separation of most groups with PC 1 carrying 65.4% of the variance.
source: This analysis showed a significant separation of most groups with PC 1 carrying 65.4% of the variance (p = 0.001, PERMANOVA).
evidence: The claim is supported by principal component analysis with statistical testing.

claim: P. brassicae caterpillars, P. brassicae caterpillar spit, C. glomerata female wasps, and caterpillar frass treatment groups were clearly separated.
source: P. brassicae caterpillars (Pb, n = 10), P. brassicae caterpillar spit (Pb-S, n = 12), C. glomerata female wasps (Cg, n = 12), and caterpillar frass (Pb-Fr, n = 10) treatment groups were clearly separated (Pb vs. Cg, Pb vs. Pb-S, Pb vs. Pb-Fr, Pb-S vs. Cg, and Pb-Fr vs. Cg, p = 0.0013; Pb-S vs. Pb-Fr, p = 0.0022 pairwise PERMANOVA, Figure 3A)
evidence: The claim is supported by principal component analysis with pairwise PERMANOVA testing shown in Figure 3A.

claim: The identified and measured volatile blend from Pb was similar to that of the P. brassicae caterpillars–C. glomerata parasitoids combination.
source: whereas the identified and measured volatile blend from Pb was similar to that of the P. brassicae caterpillars–C. glomerata parasitoids combination (Pb–Cg, n = 14) (p = 0.0330, pairwise PERMANOVA).
evidence: The claim is supported by principal component analysis with pairwise PERMANOVA testing.

claim: Most of the identified compounds were found in significantly higher amounts in Pb-S and/or Pb-Fr compared to the other treatments.
source: Most of the identified compounds were found in significantly higher amounts in Pb-S and/or Pb-Fr compared to the other treatments (Figure 3B, Supplementary file 1A).
evidence: The claim is supported by quantitative volatile analysis shown in Figure 3B and Supplementary file 1A.

claim: WT caterpillars displayed a preference for two plant chemicals, namely (Z)-3-hexen-1-ol and (E)-2-hexenal over paraffin oil.
source: The results showed that WT caterpillars displayed a preference for two plant chemicals, namely (Z)-3-hexen-1-ol and (E)-2-hexenal over paraffin oil (p = 0.0482 and p = 0.0321) (Figure 3D).
evidence: The claim is supported by behavioral assay data with statistical testing shown in Figure 3D.

claim: KO caterpillars did not exhibit any significant attraction or avoidance behavior toward the tested chemicals.
source: In contrast, KO caterpillars did not exhibit any significant attraction or avoidance behavior toward the tested chemicals (Figure 3E).
evidence: The claim is supported by behavioral assay data shown in Figure 3E.

claim: WT caterpillars were more active in the arena, moving around.
source: Additionally, we found that WT caterpillars were more active in the arena, moving around (Figure 3—figure supplement 6)
evidence: The claim is supported by behavioral tracking data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 6.

claim: KO caterpillars were less active in the arena, often remaining at the same position within the channels.
source: while KO caterpillars were less active in the arena, often remaining at the same position within the channels (Figure 3—figure supplement 7).
evidence: The claim is supported by behavioral tracking data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 7.

claim: Chemoreception plays a critical role in the insect life cycle.
source: Chemoreception plays a critical role in the insect life cycle.
evidence: The claim is a general statement supported by established scientific knowledge.

claim: Insects exploit chemical cues to locate food plants, to find and select mates, to evaluate oviposition sites, and to avoid natural enemies.
source: For instance, insects exploit chemical cues to locate food plants, to find and select mates, to evaluate oviposition sites, and to avoid natural enemies (Dicke and Grostal, 2001).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to previous research.

claim: Olfaction has been extensively investigated in many species.
source: Olfaction, a pivotal component of chemoreception, involves multiple processes in insects and has been extensively investigated in many species (Haverkamp et al., 2018)
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to previous research.

claim: The study of olfaction in insects has largely centered upon imagos, the final life stage of insects.
source: Thus far, the study of olfaction in insects has largely centered upon imagos, the final life stage of insects.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from the literature review.

claim: The olfactory system in larval herbivores remains largely unexplored.
source: Nonetheless, the olfactory system in larval herbivores remains largely unexplored.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from the literature review.

claim: Chemoreception is considered to play an important role in tri-trophic systems.
source: Tri-trophic interactions among plants, herbivores, and natural enemies have been widely investigated in the last few decades, and chemoreception is considered to play an important role in these systems (Vet and Dicke, 1992; Turlings and Erb, 2018).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: Olfactory information, such as plant volatiles, is crucial in the coevolution of herbivores and natural enemies.
source: In particular, abundant research has demonstrated that olfactory information, such as plant volatiles, is crucial in the coevolution of herbivores and natural enemies (Turlings and Erb, 2018; Dicke and Baldwin, 2010; Haverkamp and Smid, 2020).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: Chemicals emitted by the insects themselves also play an important role in tri-trophic interactions.
source: In addition to plant volatiles, chemicals emitted by the insects themselves also play an important role (Venugopal et al., 2020; Ebrahim et al., 2015).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: Drosophila melanogaster fruit flies prefer to lay eggs on citrus fruits because the volatiles emitted by citrus are repellent to the endoparasitoid Leptopilina boulardi.
source: Drosophila melanogaster fruit flies, for example, prefer to lay eggs on citrus fruits because the volatiles emitted by citrus are repellent to the endoparasitoid Leptopilina boulardi, a natural enemy of fruit fly larvae (Dweck et al., 2013).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to previous research.

claim: The brown planthopper Nilaparvata lugens deposits eggs on rice plants infested by the striped stem borer Chilo suppressalis, which is repellent to the egg parasitoid Anagrus nilaparvatae.
source: Similarly, the brown planthopper Nilaparvata lugens deposits eggs on rice plants infested by the striped stem borer Chilo suppressalis, which is repellent to the egg parasitoid Anagrus nilaparvatae (Hu et al., 2020).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to previous research.

claim: Insect olfaction is dominated by two classes of olfactory receptor genes, odorant receptors (ORs) and ionotropic receptors (IRs).
source: Insect olfaction is dominated by two classes of olfactory receptor genes, odorant receptors (ORs) and ionotropic receptors (IRs).
evidence: The claim is based on established scientific knowledge.

claim: ORs detect the majority of volatiles in the insect habitat.
source: ORs detect the majority of volatiles in the insect habitat.
evidence: The claim is based on established scientific knowledge.

claim: In all ORs, the odorant receptor co-receptor (Orco) is required to form a functional ion channel in the membrane of the odorant receptor neurons (ORNs).
source: In all ORs, the odorant receptor co-receptor (Orco) is required to form a functional ion channel in the membrane of the odorant receptor neurons (ORNs) (Sato et al., 2008; Wicher et al., 2008; Jones et al., 2005).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: Silencing the Orco gene can lead to a severe olfaction deficiency, causing a loss of social behavior, impaired mating, and significantly reduced foraging behavior.
source: Previous research indicates that silencing the Orco gene can lead to a severe olfaction deficiency, causing a loss of social behavior, impaired mating, and significantly reduced foraging behavior (Trible et al., 2017; Yan et al., 2017; Fandino et al., 2019).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: Adult insect behavior and neuronal development were greatly affected when Orco is knocked out.
source: Previous reports have also clearly shown that adult insect behavior and neuronal development were greatly affected when Orco is knocked out (Trible et al., 2017; Yan et al., 2017).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: Potential changes in olfaction-deficient larvae remain largely unexplored.
source: Yet, potential changes in olfaction-deficient larvae remain largely unexplored, and little is known about how olfaction contributes to the co-adaptation of larvae and their natural enemies, especially in the larvae of non-model insects such as lepidopteran caterpillars.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from the literature review.

claim: Little is known about how olfaction contributes to the co-adaptation of larvae and their natural enemies, especially in the larvae of non-model insects such as lepidopteran caterpillars.
source: Yet, potential changes in olfaction-deficient larvae remain largely unexplored, and little is known about how olfaction contributes to the co-adaptation of larvae and their natural enemies, especially in the larvae of non-model insects such as lepidopteran caterpillars.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from the literature review.

claim: Pieris brassicae is a very common butterfly species that causes substantial agricultural production loss across Europe and the Indian subcontinent.
source: Pieris brassicae is a very common butterfly species that causes substantial agricultural production loss across Europe and the Indian subcontinent (Feltwell, 1982; Hasan and Ansari, 2011; Hasan and Shafiq Ansari, 2010).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: The butterflies utilize chemoreception to evaluate oviposition sites and host plants.
source: The butterflies utilize chemoreception to evaluate oviposition sites and host plants (van Loon et al., 1992a; van Loon et al., 1992b; Wang et al., 2023).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: The caterpillars have a well-developed olfactory system.
source: The caterpillars also have a well-developed olfactory system (Wang et al., 2024)
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to previous research.

claim: Chemical communication has been demonstrated to be involved in the interaction between herbivores and their natural enemies.
source: and chemical communication has been demonstrated to be involved in the interaction between herbivores and their natural enemies (Stam et al., 2014; Dicke and Baldwin, 2010).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: Natural enemies such as parasitoid wasps are highly attracted to volatiles from cabbage plants infested by P. brassicae caterpillars.
source: Natural enemies such as parasitoid wasps are highly attracted to volatiles from cabbage plants infested by P. brassicae caterpillars (Mattiacci et al., 1994).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to previous research.

claim: P. brassicae caterpillars can defend themselves by spitting at natural enemies while being attacked.
source: P. brassicae caterpillars are thus under strong selection pressure from natural enemies, though caterpillars can defend themselves by spitting at natural enemies while being attacked (Müller et al., 2003).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to previous research.

claim: The loss of olfactory glomeruli in the caterpillar might indicate that the formation of glomeruli in the embryo is mediated by a different mechanism than during pupation.
source: The loss of olfactory glomeruli in the caterpillar might, therefore, either indicate that the formation of glomeruli in the embryo is mediated by a different mechanism than during pupation (Oland and Tolbert, 2011), or that the loss of neuronal activity reduces axonal innervations and thereby the size of the glomeruli to an extent that they could no longer be visualized by our method.
evidence: The claim is speculative reasoning about the mechanism underlying glomeruli loss, citing previous work on glomerular formation.

claim: The loss of neuronal activity reduces axonal innervations and thereby the size of the glomeruli to an extent that they could no longer be visualized by the method used.
source: The loss of olfactory glomeruli in the caterpillar might, therefore, either indicate that the formation of glomeruli in the embryo is mediated by a different mechanism than during pupation (Oland and Tolbert, 2011), or that the loss of neuronal activity reduces axonal innervations and thereby the size of the glomeruli to an extent that they could no longer be visualized by our method.
evidence: The claim is speculative reasoning about the mechanism underlying glomeruli loss.

claim: Additional sensory systems beyond olfaction, such as vision, may be involved in the mating processes of this day-active butterfly.
source: This finding suggests that additional sensory systems beyond olfaction, such as vision, may be involved in the mating processes of this day-active butterfly (Carpenter and Sparks, 1982; Obara et al., 2008).
evidence: The claim is inference based on the observation that KO butterflies still mate, supported by citations to previous research on butterfly mating.

claim: Oviposition decisions are mostly guided by non-volatile compounds when no host-plant location is required.
source: The mated Orco KO butterflies laid a comparable number of fertilized eggs on cabbage plants to WT butterflies, which is in line with the results from different moth species (Fandino et al., 2019; Fan et al., 2022; Sun et al., 2023), suggesting oviposition decisions are mostly guided by non-volatile compounds when no host-plant location is required (van Loon et al., 1992a).
evidence: The claim is inference based on the observation that KO butterflies lay similar numbers of eggs when plants are provided, supported by citations to previous research.

claim: The reduced fecundity in these insects is primarily due to impaired mating behavior and reduced mating frequency, which may result from a lack of pheromonal communication.
source: Furthermore, the hatching rate of eggs laid by mated Orco KO butterflies was similar to that of WT butterflies (Figure 1—figure supplement 2), indicating that the reduced fecundity in these insects is primarily due to impaired mating behavior and reduced mating frequency, which may result from a lack of pheromonal communication.
evidence: The claim is inference based on the observation that hatching rates are similar but mating frequency is reduced, shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2.

claim: Olfaction is needed to evaluate plant tissues and to select different leaves or leaf parts in order to feed efficiently, even when the caterpillar is already on the plant.
source: We speculate that olfaction is needed to evaluate plant tissues and to select different leaves or leaf parts in order to feed efficiently, even when the caterpillar is already on the plant.
evidence: The claim is speculation based on the observation that KO caterpillars gain less weight than WT caterpillars on plants.

claim: Secondary metabolites are often unevenly distributed even within a single leaf, and these concentration differences have been shown to influence the performance of different caterpillars.
source: Secondary metabolites are often unevenly distributed even within a single leaf, and these concentration differences have been shown to influence the performance of different caterpillars (Kester et al., 2002; Yuan et al., 2022).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: Localized differences in plant secondary metabolites are detectable by the herbivore through its olfactory system.
source: It is conceivable that these localized differences in plant secondary metabolites are also detectable by the herbivore through its olfactory system (Hanson and Dethier, 1973).

claim: The further reduction in caterpillar weight in the presence of disarmed parasitoids was due to the less efficient foraging behavior of the KO caterpillars.
